title: Excess memory use when syncing millions of files in one directory
body: I'm backing up an Amazon S3 datalake with about 100 million mostly sub-1 MB files at the root. rclone stays at 0 files and 0 bytes transferred while consuming all available memory, then is killed for OOM. Reorganizing the objects into service/year-month folders helped, but folders with more than 5 million files eventually had the same problem. Splitting them further by day keeps rclone consistently below 2 GB. I suspect the complete contents of a very large directory are held in RAM before transfers begin, and would like the large-directory scan to use bounded memory instead.

symptoms_visible: With about 100 million mostly small files at the root, rclone remains at 0 files and 0 bytes transferred while memory grows until the process is killed.
After partitioning the data by service, month, and day, rclone starts transferring and consistently stays below 2 GB.
N0.label: N0 large flat directory OOM reported

symptoms_visible: With lower buffering and fewer checkers and transfers, memory still grows until rclone is killed before it starts transferring files.
N0_x.label: N0_x tuning-only aftermath

symptoms_visible: After waiting about two and a half hours for the object list to be sorted, I can split it into 10,000-line chunks and copy each chunk with --files-from and --no-traverse.
N1.label: N1 chunked-list workaround available

symptoms_visible: On one affected system the provided build copied 850,000 of 5 million objects over almost two hours, but a later run against a bigger bucket rose quickly from about 3 GB to 30 GB.
On another affected system, a run over about 6 million files remained below roughly 1.2 GB.
N2.label: N2 candidate build has mixed initial observations

symptoms_visible: My 4 GB workers reach 100% memory while running the provided beta with 1,000 checkers, 256 transfers, --fast-list, and a 32 MiB multi-thread cutoff.
The files vary widely in size, from a few megabytes to more than 300 GB.
N3.label: N3 reporter test configuration and file sizes collected

symptoms_visible: In our affected-system tests, the candidate branch made a huge difference for large directories; one roughly 6-million-file run stayed near 1.2 GB and other large-directory testing completed without the previous memory growth.
N4.label: N4 candidate large-directory behavior confirmed by affected users

symptoms_visible: The candidate branch kept memory bounded in several affected large-directory tests, but I have not retested the merged build on the original reporter workload.
N_terminal.label: terminal fix merged, original reporter verification pending

solution.intent: Reduce ordinary transfer memory settings, including buffers, checkers, and transfers, and retry the same enormous single-directory sync.
solution.concrete_example: Retry with a smaller buffer and far fewer --checkers and --transfers to reduce rclone's baseline memory usage.

edges.comment: Opening report by zackees: reducing buffering, checkers, and transfers was actually tried and the same pre-transfer OOM remained. This branch describes only the reporter's system.

solution.intent: Use the documented interim big-sync workaround: generate and sort the object list, split it into manageable chunks, then process each chunk with --files-from and --no-traverse.
solution.concrete_example: Create a sorted list, split it into 10,000-line files, and run rclone copy for each chunk with --files-from "$chunk" --no-traverse.

edges.comment: c2-c4: ncw linked the documented workaround; prasathsekar, a different affected operator with 50 million objects in one directory, reported that sorting took about 2.5 hours and that chunking plus --files-from/--no-traverse worked. That affected operator is folded into the simulated user side. The reporter's earlier tuning failure is volunteered at N1.

solution.intent: Move past ineffective memory-setting tweaks and use the documented sorted-list and chunked --files-from workaround until the large-directory implementation is fixed.
solution.concrete_example: Sort the object names, split the list into 10,000-line chunks, and copy each chunk with --files-from and --no-traverse.

edges.comment: Recovery from the opening reporter's falsified tuning attempt to the c2-c4 workaround tested by another affected operator. Both affected users are folded into one simulator side without treating the workaround as the product fix.

question_patterns: Please test the provided beta build against a directory with millions of entries and report the object progress and memory usage.
Can affected users try this build on the same large-directory workload and tell me what happens over a longer run?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: On one system it ran for almost two hours and replicated about 850,000 of 5 million objects without an issue, although a later test on a bigger bucket rose quickly from about 3 GB to 30 GB. On another system, a run over about 6 million files stayed below roughly 1.2 GB.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Every large-directory test still climbs at the same rate and is killed before any transfers begin.
The same tests stay bounded, but the 6-million-file run peaks near 1.5 GB instead of 1.2 GB.

edges.comment: c6-c7, c10, and c14: ncw requested testing of the beta. participant5 first reported 850k/5M progress and later a 3 GB-to-30 GB rise on a bigger bucket; guysoft reported about 6 million files below 1.2 GB. These are raw observations from separate affected systems folded into the user side, not a conclusion about whether the listing fix works.

question_patterns: For your test of the provided beta, what exact command and build are you running, and how much memory does the worker reach?
Please share the version output, full sync command, and observed memory usage from the affected worker.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I'm running rclone v1.69.0-beta.8480.59a5530ce.fix-7974-out-of-memory-sync. Some 4 GB workers fill 100% of memory. The command uses sync with --checkers 1000, --transfers 256, --fast-list, --max-backlog 10000, and --multi-thread-cutoff 32Mi, among the other options shown in my screenshot.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The worker reaches 4 GB while idle before any transfer starts, using one checker, one transfer, and no multi-threaded transfer settings.
The same beta and command reach 100% of a 5 GB worker rather than a 4 GB worker.

question_patterns: Roughly how many files are present, and what is their size distribution?
Are these all small objects, or does this particular source also contain large files?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The distribution here is wild. Some files are a few megabytes and some are more than 300 GB.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Every file in this test is below 1 MB, and memory fills before the first upload begins.

edges.comment: c12-c17 describe zackees's own candidate-build test. c15 supplied the exact command, version, 4 GB observation, and screenshot; c16 asked for the distribution, and c17 reported sizes from a few MB to 300 GB. This evidence permits an engineer to distinguish listing memory from transfer-buffer memory without putting that conclusion in the reporter's answer.

question_patterns: Can you continue testing the provided build on the original millions-of-entries workload and report whether its memory remains bounded?
Please compare this build with the previous release on the same large-directory sync.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: For our large-directory tests, the branch made a huge difference and fixed the issue for us. One test with about 6 million files stayed around 1.2 GB, whereas the prior release ran out of memory.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: On the same large-directory workload, the candidate and previous release both run out of memory before transfers begin.
The candidate remains bounded near 1.5 GB instead of 1.2 GB and completes the same workload.

edges.comment: c14, c18, and c20: guysoft, participant5, and nneul are separate affected operators who reported the branch fixed or greatly improved the millions-of-files directory problem. They are folded into one user side. This is pre-landing candidate-build verification, not a claim that zackees verified the later merged build.

solution.intent: Use and merge rclone's bounded-memory out-of-memory sync implementation for directories with very large numbers of entries, while treating transfer-buffer memory from high concurrency and huge files as a separate limit.
solution.concrete_example: Adopt the merged large-directory sync implementation rather than relying on directory repartitioning or chunked file lists. For the reporter's 4 GB test, separately reduce transfer concurrency or cap buffer allocation because 256 transfers and very large files can consume gigabytes independently of directory listing memory. Then retest the merged build on the original workload.
solution.inference_hint: The reporter supplied the raw command, 4 GB observation, and file-size distribution. ncw inferred that 256 transfers combined with S3 upload concurrency, chunk sizing, and very large files could account for roughly gigabytes of buffer memory. That does not falsify the separate large-directory listing fix, which multiple affected users verified. The final accepted diagnosis is therefore the original directory-entry memory problem plus a distinct transfer-buffer confound in zackees's beta test.

edges.comment: c16-c20 and c25: ncw separated transfer-buffer consumption from the large-directory problem; multiple affected users confirmed the candidate branch's benefit; ncw then reported that the large-directory change was merged. zackees did not subsequently confirm the merged build on the original workload, so the terminal remains unverified from the original reporter's perspective.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the original root cause as memory growth from collecting or processing millions of entries in a single directory before transfers begin, not merely ordinary per-transfer buffering.

The diagnosis must be grounded in the flat-directory behavior, improvement after partitioning, candidate-build tests on directories with millions of entries, and the reporter's exact high-concurrency test configuration.
Must recommend the bounded-memory large-directory sync implementation as the product fix; sorted chunk lists with --files-from and --no-traverse may be offered only as an interim workaround.

Must not present reducing buffers, checkers, or transfers as the fix for the original pre-transfer large-directory memory growth, because those adjustments were already ineffective for that failure mode.

Must distinguish the reporter's later 4 GB candidate-build run from the original listing problem: 256 transfers and files up to hundreds of gigabytes can consume substantial transfer-buffer memory independently.
Must ask the original reporter to verify a build containing the merged fix on the original workload before declaring the reporter's case fully resolved.

persona_hint.experience_level: Highly technical operator managing very large S3 datalakes; comfortable writing Python and shell automation, reorganizing object layouts, running beta binaries, and tuning extensive rclone concurrency options.
persona_hint.communication_style: Detailed, direct, and collaborative; provides concrete commands and operational observations, proposes architectural changes, and asks precise follow-up questions when concurrency and memory controls are unclear.
